_ssot: Rulings only -- no machine paths and no scan output. Paths live in the gitignored sites.local.json so any clone works in any directory; frozen hashes are never stored because a hash that disagrees with reality is worse than no record at all.
_rule: A skill is either shared infrastructure (exactly one copy, here, reached from every project through the user-level surfaces) or repo-owned (differentiated on purpose, living in that repo's big loop). Nothing is both. A repo holding its own copy of a shared name shadows the shared one silently -- that is what `check` exists to catch. A third state exists as of 2026-08-07: a name can be deliberately repo-owned in several repos at once. That is not shadowing -- nothing shared is being hidden -- so `check` must not report it as drift.

shared.name: shared-skills-infra
shared.why: The governance tool has to sit under its own rule, or the one skill that can detect shadowing is the one nothing checks.

shared.name: github-delivery-loop
shared.why: Merge authority is host infrastructure, not repo policy: the same four-layer stack and the same two hosts gate every repo. It was already split into a v0.1 and a v1.1, and that split is precisely why the same blockers kept recurring.

shared.name: autoresearch-composer

shared.name: gitlab-delivery-loop
shared.why: Same reason as its GitHub sibling: merge authority is host infrastructure, not repo policy -- the same four-layer stack and the same two hosts gate every repo. Kept as a separate name rather than a --host flag on github-delivery-loop because the two forges must not be interchangeable at run time; the split is enforced by disjoint schemas, disjoint identity fields and a cross-forge refusal test, not by documentation.

shared.name: knowledge-continuity
shared.why: Only ix-agy had it, and nothing in it is about ix-agy. A skill that one repo happens to have written is not thereby repo-owned.

shared.name: repo-fullstack-debugger
shared.why: Two repos, two lines of difference. The antigravity copy was the superset -- it carried the note on when to hand off to a different model family instead.

shared.name: forgejo-delivery-loop
shared.why: bettor-arena holds the mechanism; the ts-skill-bettor copy says so itself in its own header, which makes it a binding, not a second body. Kept separate from the GitHub and GitLab siblings by the earlier ruling: the forges must not be interchangeable at run time. 2026-08-07: absorbed forgejo-loop-ops, which was the operations half of the same loop -- one skill said which line to work, the other how to move it without leaving half-applied state, and splitting them made 'which one first' a question you had to answer every time. Its router, cases and contracts moved in whole; the selftest still runs 19/19.

shared.name: loop-harness-standard
shared.why: Five copies. skill-bettor's is the evolved one (bettor-arena and ts-skill-bettor hold verbatim older copies of it), so it is the body; ix-agy's architecture SSOT module and antigravity's reference implementation fold in, minus the vendored venv.

shared.name: repo-wiki-converge
shared.why: Four copies. ix-agy's module had four operational fixes the others never learned -- monorepo git detection, judge timeout, and the zero-page hole where a mechanical checker passed because there was no code to fail. Exactly the rediscovery this repo exists to stop.

repo_owned.name: harness-wiki
repo_owned.why: It is a map of one repo's loops. Three repos held it and every single file differed, because the thing it describes differs. Sharing it would leave a body that is all skeleton and a binding that is all content.

repo_owned.name: product-ops
repo_owned.why: Same as harness-wiki: an operating runbook for one repo's own factory.

repo_owned.name: skill-authoring
repo_owned.why: House rules, which are the part each repo is entitled to differ on. The generic half already lives in the built-in write-a-skill.
